newsitem.title: USA: Daschle asks bipartisan support on campaign reform.
newsitem.headline: Daschle asks bipartisan support on campaign reform.

text.p: Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle Wednesday asked Republicans to work with Democrats in the first 60 days of the new Congress to reform the controversial and costly financing of political campaigns.

"Nothing would send a stronger message to the American people than on a bipartisan basis we're going to clean up the system (in time for the next elections)," the South Dakota Democrat told a news conference.

The two political parties raised unprecedented amounts of cash for this year's election, especially "soft money" -- an unlimited channel for businesses, unions and wealthy people to funnel money into politics without regard to federal limits.
That money is supposed to be for getting out the vote and party building but is routinely used for television ads backing particular candidates.

All sides deplored the process even as they rushed to collect and spend money as quickly as possible. Federal Election Comission figures show the Republican Party raised $121 million of soft money in the 21 months starting in 1995 and the Democrats $102 million.
Daschle said all that should end. "The soft money is very simple. You just ban it. It is a gargantuan loophole."
The controversy over campaign financing is not simple, however, and there is every indication a deadlock that began early last summer has not been broken.

When the Senate considered a bipartisan bill to outlaw soft money, while both parties were in a fundraising frenzy, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott led a filibuster killing it. Lott and other Republicans demanded that any campaign finance reform bill clip the wings of unions, which use dues money in political campaigns unless members object in writing.

Daschle and other Democrats, who benefited from the union money, called that a "non-starter." Democrats say if unions are to be limited in their contributions then corporations -- whose donations favour Republicans -- should be limited too.

Republicans plan to hold a series of hearings on campaign financing abuses, starting with the highest-profile fundraiser for the Democratic National Committee, John Huang. Huang was recently fired from his job, but not before he brought in $2.5 million for the party -- of which nearly $600,000 had to be returned as illegal.

Another issue is independent expenditures, which Daschle said, without being specific, must be addressed. The Supreme Court ruled last June that parties have a constitutional free speech right to make unlimited "independent expenditures" if they are not coordinated with campaigns.
